problem: Find the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x)=\frac{14{x}^{3}}{6{x}^{3}+1}.$

feedback.problem:
What is the horizontal asymptote of $y=f(x)$ for $x>0$ with $f(x)=\frac{|3-8x|}{4x+1}?$

The horizontal asymptote is $y=$

{{field-1}}.
feedback.worked_solution:
For large positive values of $x,$ we have $|3-8x|=8x-3.$ Consequently, for $x\to \infty ,$ we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{|3-8x|}{4x+1}={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{8x-3}{4x+1}.
$$

The horizontal asymptote for $x>0$ is $y={lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{8x-3}{4x+1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{8x}{x}-\frac{3}{x})}{(\frac{4x}{x}+\frac{1}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(8-\frac{3}{x})}{(4+\frac{1}{x})} \\  & =\frac{8-0}{4+0} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the horizontal asymptote is $y=2.$
